subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look up. Every single day of your life, the Sun climbs into the sky over the Indian Ocean, warms the savanna, and later slips down behind the western hills. Every month the Moon grows from a thin silver curve into a bright full circle, then shrinks away again. When your family watches for the new crescent moon to know that Ramadan or Eid has begun, you are doing exactly what scientists and travellers have done for thousands of years — reading the sky. In this unit you are going to discover the real story behind these everyday wonders.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Explore, through modeling, that the sun does not move; its apparent movement is caused by the Earth spinning on its axis
Know that the Earth spins on its axis once in every 24 hours
Know that the Earth takes a year to orbit the sun, spinning as it goes

objectives.subStrand: Obtain and present evidence; Consider evidence and approach

outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Explain that Earth is a planet that travels around the Sun, together with seven other planets in our Solar System.
Describe how Earth spinning on its axis causes the cycle of day and night.
Explain why the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, even though the Sun is not really moving around us.
Describe how Earth's journey around the Sun takes one year (about 365 days).
Explain why the Moon appears to change shape through its phases, and connect this to the lunar (Hijri) calendar.
Name the eight planets in order and describe how the Solar System is arranged.
Use the Sun and stars to work out direction, and understand how people have navigated with the sky.
Carry out safe home investigations using a ball and a torch to model day, night and the Moon's phases.
Here are the important words for this unit. Say each one aloud, then use it when you talk about the sky with your family or your AI tutor.

concepts.title: Our Home in Space
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with a big question: what is your address in the universe? You might start with your house, then your town — perhaps Mogadishu, Kismaayo or Dar es Salaam — then your country, then the continent of Africa. But you can keep going. Africa sits on the planet Earth. Earth is one of eight planets that travel around a star we call the Sun. The Sun and everything travelling around it make up our Solar System. And our Solar System is just one tiny corner of a giant collection of billions of stars called a galaxy. That is a very big address!

At the centre of our Solar System sits the Sun. The Sun is a star — an enormous ball of hot, glowing gas so large that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. The Sun makes its own light and heat through powerful reactions deep inside. This is why the equatorial Sun feels so strong on your skin at midday: you are standing almost directly beneath it. Everything else in the Solar System, including Earth, is much smaller and does not make its own light. Planets only reflect the Sun's light, like a wall lit by a lamp.

There are eight planets. In order from the Sun they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A helpful way to remember the order is to make up a sentence where each word begins with the same letter as a planet — try inventing your own with your AI tutor. The four planets closest to the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars) are small and made mostly of rock. The four farthest away (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune) are enormous and made mostly of gas, which is why they are called the gas giants.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun. This position is special. We are not so close that the oceans boil away, and not so far that they freeze solid. We are just the right distance for liquid water, breathable air, and life. When you drink camel milk, watch flamingos wade in a lake, or feel the coastal wind at Berbera, you are enjoying gifts that come from Earth sitting in exactly the right place in space.

Did You Know? The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away from Earth. Its light takes just over 8 minutes to reach us. So the sunrise you see over the Indian Ocean actually left the Sun 8 minutes earlier! If you could drive a car to the Sun at highway speed without stopping, the journey would take over 170 years.

How do we know Earth travels around the Sun, when it feels as if we are standing perfectly still? For a long time, most people believed the Sun moved around the Earth, because that is how it looks. But careful observers like Copernicus and Galileo studied the sky for years and used reasoning and evidence to show that Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun. This is an important lesson in science: what seems obvious to our eyes is not always the truth. We must observe carefully, gather evidence, and be willing to change our minds. Observing creation closely and thinking carefully about it is a way of growing in both knowledge and wonder.
concepts.example: Earth's path around the Sun is called its orbit. The orbit is not a perfect circle — it is a very slightly squashed circle, like an egg shape called an ellipse. But the squashing is so small that Earth stays almost the same distance from the Sun all year round. This is important: it means the seasons are not caused by Earth moving closer to or farther from the Sun. Remember that — it is one of the most common mistakes people make.

concepts.title: Day and Night: Earth's Spin
concepts.explanation:
Now think about a single day. In the morning the Sun rises in the east, over the Indian Ocean if you live on the coast. By midday it is high overhead — this is noon. In the evening it sinks in the west and sets, and then comes night. It really looks as if the Sun is travelling across the sky above us. But it is not. Here is the true explanation.

Earth spins like a top. This spinning is called rotation. Earth turns all the way around once every 24 hours, which is exactly why a day is 24 hours long. Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis, which runs straight through the planet from the North Pole to the South Pole. Picture pushing a knitting needle through an orange from top to bottom, then spinning the orange — the needle is the axis.

The Sun shines on Earth from one side only, just as a torch shines on one side of a ball. So at any moment, half of Earth is lit (that half has daytime) and half is dark (that half has night-time). As Earth rotates, your town is carried around into the light and then around into the dark, over and over. When your part of Earth turns to face the Sun, you see the Sun "rise" and you have day. When your part turns away, the Sun "sets" and you have night. The Sun never moved — you did, carried by the spinning Earth.

Because Earth spins from west to east, the Sun appears to move the opposite way, from east to west. This is just like riding in a car: when you look out of the window, the trees and houses seem to rush backwards, even though they are standing still and you are the one moving. In the same way, the whole sky seems to slide from east to west because you are riding on a turning planet.

Because Earth is round and always turning, different parts of the world have day and night at different times. When it is daytime for you, it is night-time on the far side of the planet. To help people keep track of this, the world is divided into time zones — 24 of them, one for roughly each hour of Earth's spin. This is why, when it is midday in Kampala, it is the middle of the night in countries far to the east or west. Understanding rotation helps explain a real everyday thing: why a phone call to a relative in another country might reach them while they are still sleeping.

You can even see the proof of Earth's rotation in a shadow. If you push a straight stick upright into the ground in a sunny spot and mark the tip of its shadow every hour, you will find the shadow slowly swings around and changes length through the day. Around noon, when the Sun is highest, the shadow is at its shortest. In the early morning and late afternoon, when the Sun is low, shadows stretch out long. This moving shadow is the very same idea as a sundial, the oldest kind of clock, and it is caused entirely by Earth turning.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Near the equator — across much of East Africa — day and night stay close to 12 hours each all year round. Far to the north or south, summer days can last many more hours than winter days. This is why the strong midday Sun is such a steady part of daily life close to the equator.

concepts.title: The Year: Earth's Journey Around the Sun
concepts.explanation:
While Earth is spinning to give us day and night, it is also slowly travelling all the way around the Sun. One full trip around the Sun takes about 365 days — and that is exactly what we call a year. So Earth is doing two movements at the same time: it is rotating (spinning once a day) and orbiting (circling the Sun once a year). Think of a spinning top that someone is also carrying slowly around a table.

A year is actually a little longer than 365 days — it is closer to 365 and a quarter days. Those extra quarter-days add up. Every four years we save them up into one extra whole day, the 29th of February, and that year is called a leap year. This is one clever way people keep their calendars matching Earth's real journey around the Sun.
concepts.example: Earth's axis is tilted — it leans over at an angle rather than standing straight up. As Earth journeys around the Sun, this tilt means that different parts of the planet lean towards the Sun at different times of the year. The part leaning towards the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days — that is summer. Six months later the same part leans away, getting less direct sunlight and shorter days — that is winter. This tilt, not the small change in distance, is the real cause of the seasons. Close to the equator the effect is gentle, which is why East Africa has fairly steady daylight but strong dry and wet seasons instead of the icy winters found far to the north.

concepts.title: The Moon and Its Phases
concepts.explanation:
Now let us turn to Earth's closest companion in space: the Moon. The Moon is a natural satellite, which means it travels around Earth, just as Earth travels around the Sun. The Moon is much smaller than Earth — about one quarter of Earth's width — and it is our nearest neighbour in space, though still very far away. It takes the Moon about 29.5 days to travel once around Earth.

Here is something surprising: the Moon does not make its own light. It is not glowing like the Sun. The reason the Moon looks bright is that it reflects sunlight, like a mirror or a pale stone catching the light of a lamp. At any moment, the Sun lights up one half of the Moon, and the other half is in darkness. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of its bright, sunlit half. That is what makes the Moon appear to change shape. These changing shapes are called the phases of the Moon.

Let us walk through the main phases in order. At new moon, the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, so its dark side faces us and we can barely see it at all. A day or two later, a thin bright curve appears — the waxing crescent. This slim crescent is the very sign your family looks for to announce the start of a new month in the Islamic (Hijri) calendar. The lit part then grows, or waxes, through the first quarter (when we see half of the lit side) and the waxing gibbous, until we reach the full moon, when the whole sunlit face shines back at us and the savanna is bright enough to walk by at night.

After full moon, the bright part shrinks, or wanes. We pass through the waning gibbous, the third quarter (half lit again, but the other half this time), and the waning crescent, until we return to new moon and the whole cycle begins again. The words waxing means growing and waning means shrinking. Remember: the Moon itself never changes shape or size. It is a round ball the whole time. Only the amount of its bright side that we can see from Earth changes as it orbits us.

Did You Know? The Islamic (Hijri) calendar is a lunar calendar — each month begins with the sighting of the new crescent moon. Because 12 lunar months are about 11 days shorter than a solar year, Ramadan and Eid move earlier each year on the ordinary calendar. This is why Ramadan slowly shifts through all the seasons over a person's lifetime — a beautiful pattern written into the sky.
concepts.example: Because the phases follow the same pattern every 29.5 days, they can be predicted. People have used this for thousands of years to make calendars, to plan journeys, and to know when the bright full moon would light the way for night travel across the land. The Moon also pulls gently on Earth's oceans, and this pull is one of the causes of the tides — the daily rising and falling of the sea that fishermen along the Indian Ocean coast know so well.

concepts.title: Stars, Constellations and Finding Your Way
concepts.explanation:
On a clear night far from city lights — out in the open savanna — the sky fills with countless tiny points of light. These are stars, and every one of them is a Sun of its own: a huge ball of hot, glowing gas making its own light. They look tiny only because they are unimaginably far away. Light from even the nearest star (after our Sun) takes more than four years to reach your eyes. Our Sun looks big and bright only because it is so much closer to us than all the others.

Long ago, people noticed that certain stars form patterns in the sky. We call these patterns constellations. The stars in a constellation are not really close together — some are far behind others — but from where we stand on Earth they make a shape we can recognise. Different cultures have seen different pictures and told different stories about the same stars. This is part of the rich human habit of looking up and finding meaning and beauty in creation.

Stars, like the Sun, seem to move slowly across the sky through the night, rising in the east and setting in the west. Once again, this is because Earth is rotating, not because the stars are moving around us. And because Earth also travels around the Sun through the year, we face different parts of space in different seasons, so different constellations are visible at different times of the year.

For as long as people have travelled, they have used the sky to find direction. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, giving you a rough compass every single day. At night, certain stars point the way. Sailors crossing the Indian Ocean, caravans crossing the semi-arid land, and travellers everywhere have read the stars to stay on course. This skill also helped people work out the direction of the qibla for prayer when they were far from home. Even today, the satellites of the GPS system that guide cars and ships still depend on a careful understanding of Earth's rotation and the positions of objects in the sky.
concepts.example: Did You Know? People built simple star-knowledge into daily life long before modern instruments. By knowing where the Sun sets, you always know west — and from west you can find north, south and east. The clear, dark skies of the savanna are among the best places on Earth to see the stars, because there is little city light to hide them.

concepts.title: Exploring Space
concepts.explanation:
How do we know so much about places we can never visit? People have built clever tools to explore space. Telescopes gather and focus light so we can see distant objects far more clearly than with our eyes alone. Some telescopes sit on the ground; others have been launched above the air, where the view is even sharper. Satellites are machines that we send to orbit Earth. Weather satellites help forecasters warn coastal towns like Mombasa and Kismaayo about storms; communication satellites carry phone calls and the internet across the world; and other satellites watch over forests, farmland and the changing climate.

We also send spacecraft far out into the Solar System. Robots called rovers have driven across the surface of Mars, taking photographs and studying the rocks. Astronauts live and work aboard the International Space Station, floating in orbit high above us. Space is a harsh place — there is no air to breathe, temperatures are extreme, and radiation is dangerous — so every spacecraft must be carefully designed to protect the people and machines inside. Exploring space is difficult and expensive, but it has given us many useful things, from accurate weather forecasts to the navigation that guides ships safely home.

Sending messages across space is slow because of the enormous distances. A radio signal from a rover on Mars can take several minutes to reach Earth, so we cannot steer it moment by moment as we would a toy car — the machine has to be clever enough to make many decisions on its own. This is one reason space robots are built to be so careful and independent. When you think about how far away these machines are, and how well they still work, it is a remarkable achievement of human curiosity and patience.
concepts.example: Space technology also quietly helps everyday life in East Africa. Satellites watch the movement of clouds and rain, helping to warn people about drought and floods so families and herders can prepare. They track the health of farmland and grazing land from far above, and they carry the phone and internet signals that connect distant towns. Studying the sky is not only about far-off wonders — it also protects and connects people right here at home.

methods.title: Making Day and Night With a Ball and a Torch
methods.example: To model how Earth's spinning causes day and night, and why the Sun seems to move across the sky.
steps: Make the room as dark as you can. Ask an adult to help.
Put a sticker (or draw a small dot) on the ball. This spot is your town, for example Mogadishu.
Hold the torch still and shine it on one side of the ball from about an arm's length away. This is the Sun's light.
Notice that only the side facing the torch is lit. That side has day; the shadowed side has night.
Slowly turn the ball from left to right (west to east), keeping the torch still.

methods.title: Modelling the Phases of the Moon
methods.example: To model how the Moon appears to change shape, and to see why the Moon has phases like the crescent that marks the start of a Hijri month.
steps: Darken the room. Place the lamp on a table, or ask someone to hold the torch, shining steadily from one side of the room.
Stand in the middle. Your head is Earth. Hold the pale ball out at arm's length — this is the Moon.
Turn to face the lamp and hold the ball up towards it. The lit side of the ball faces away from you — this is the NEW MOON (you see almost no light).
Slowly turn on the spot, carrying the ball around your head. Watch a thin lit curve appear on one edge — this is the WAXING CRESCENT.
Keep turning. When you have turned a quarter way round, you see half the ball lit — FIRST QUARTER.

methods.title: The Travelling Shadow (A Home Sundial)
methods.example: To show that Earth's rotation makes shadows move and change length through the day, without ever looking at the Sun.
steps: Early in the morning, stand the stick upright in a sunny spot where it will stay all day. Do NOT move it.
Look only at the SHADOW — never at the Sun. Place a small stone at the very tip of the shadow and note the time.
Every hour or two, come back and mark the new position of the shadow tip with another stone, writing the time beside it.
Continue through the day — morning, midday, and afternoon.
At the end of the day, look at the row of marks and the lengths of the shadows.

methods.title: Keeping a Moon Diary
methods.example: To observe the real Moon over several weeks and discover the pattern of its phases with your own eyes.
steps: Each clear evening, go outside with an adult after sunset and find the Moon.
Draw the exact shape of the lit part of the Moon that you can see.
Write the date beside your drawing, and note roughly what time it was.
Repeat every clear night for at least two weeks — longer is even better.
If a night is cloudy, simply write 'cloudy' and try again the next night.

workedExamples.title: Thinking With Numbers
workedExamples.prompt: Earth and space are full of patterns you can work out with simple arithmetic. Let us do some together, step by step.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1 — How many degrees does Earth turn each hour?

Earth makes one full turn — that is 360 degrees — in 24 hours. To find how much it turns in one hour, we divide:

360 degrees divided by 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour.

So every hour, Earth spins 15 degrees, and the Sun appears to move 15 degrees across the sky. This is the reason each time zone is about 15 degrees of longitude wide.

workedExamples.title: 1 - How many degrees does Earth turn each hour?
workedExamples.prompt: Earth makes one full turn — that is 360 degrees — in 24 hours. To find how much it turns in one hour, we divide:
workedExamples.solution:
360 degrees divided by 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour.

So every hour, Earth spins 15 degrees, and the Sun appears to move 15 degrees across the sky. This is the reason each time zone is about 15 degrees of longitude wide.

Worked Example 2 — How long until the next full moon?

The Moon's full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. Suppose tonight is a new moon. A full moon happens halfway through the cycle. So we work out half of 29.5:

workedExamples.title: 2 - How long until the next full moon?
workedExamples.prompt: The Moon's full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. Suppose tonight is a new moon. A full moon happens halfway through the cycle. So we work out half of 29.5:
workedExamples.solution:
29.5 days divided by 2 = about 14.75 days, which is roughly 15 days. So the full moon will come about 15 days after the new moon. If you keep a moon diary, you can check this yourself!

Worked Example 3 — How many times does Earth spin in one year?

Earth spins once each day, and there are about 365 days in a year. So in one full journey around the Sun, Earth spins about 365 times. Written out: 1 spin per day multiplied by 365 days = 365 spins per year. That means since your last birthday, the ground beneath you has turned right around about 365 times.

Reading Comprehension — Waris Watches for the Crescent

workedExamples.solution:
Reading Comprehension — Waris Watches for the Crescent

Read this short passage carefully, then answer the questions below.

The evening after sunset, Waris climbed with her grandfather onto the flat roof of their house near Berbera. The sky over the Indian Ocean was turning from orange to deep blue. "Tonight," her grandfather said softly, "we look for the new crescent. If we see that thin curve of light, tomorrow begins a new month." Waris searched the western sky where the Sun had just set. For a while she saw nothing. Then, low and delicate, a silver sliver appeared, curved like the edge of a fingernail. "There!" she cried. Her grandfather smiled. "That is the Moon reflecting the light of the Sun that has already gone below the horizon. In a few nights it will grow fatter, and in about two weeks it will be full and bright enough to light the whole savanna." Waris thought about how the same Moon she was watching had guided travellers and marked the months for countless people before her. She decided to keep a moon diary and draw its shape every clear night.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: What is at the centre of our Solar System? (a) Earth (b) the Moon (c) the Sun (d) a galaxy
workedExamples.solution: 1 (c) the Sun. The Sun sits at the centre and everything else orbits it.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin around once? (a) 1 hour (b) 24 hours (c) 1 month (d) 1 year
workedExamples.solution: 2 (b) 24 hours. One full spin (rotation) takes 24 hours, which is why a day is 24 hours.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: What causes day and night? (a) the Sun moving around Earth (b) Earth spinning on its axis (c) clouds covering the Sun (d) the Moon blocking the Sun
workedExamples.solution: 3 (b) Earth spinning on its axis. As Earth turns, your side faces the Sun (day) then turns away (night).

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun? (a) one day (b) one week (c) one month (d) about one year
workedExamples.solution: 4 (d) about one year. One orbit of the Sun takes about 365 days.

activities.title: Making Day and Night With a Ball and a Torch
activities.materials: A ball (an orange, a round fruit, or any ball) to be Earth; A torch, or a phone light, to be the Sun; A small sticker or a dot of marker pen to mark your town; A darkened room
steps: Make the room as dark as you can. Ask an adult to help.
Put a sticker (or draw a small dot) on the ball. This spot is your town, for example Mogadishu.
Hold the torch still and shine it on one side of the ball from about an arm's length away. This is the Sun's light.
Notice that only the side facing the torch is lit. That side has day; the shadowed side has night.
Slowly turn the ball from left to right (west to east), keeping the torch still.

activities.title: Modelling the Phases of the Moon
activities.materials: A small pale ball (a white or light-coloured ball, or a ball wrapped in white paper) to be the Moon; A bright torch or lamp to be the Sun; A darkened room; Your own head, which will stand for Earth
steps: Darken the room. Place the lamp on a table, or ask someone to hold the torch, shining steadily from one side of the room.
Stand in the middle. Your head is Earth. Hold the pale ball out at arm's length — this is the Moon.
Turn to face the lamp and hold the ball up towards it. The lit side of the ball faces away from you — this is the NEW MOON (you see almost no light).
Slowly turn on the spot, carrying the ball around your head. Watch a thin lit curve appear on one edge — this is the WAXING CRESCENT.
Keep turning. When you have turned a quarter way round, you see half the ball lit — FIRST QUARTER.

activities.title: The Travelling Shadow (A Home Sundial)
activities.materials: A straight stick, pencil or stone that stands upright; A sunny patch of ground or a piece of paper on a sunny windowsill; Small stones or a pencil to mark the shadow tip; A watch or clock
steps: Early in the morning, stand the stick upright in a sunny spot where it will stay all day. Do NOT move it.
Look only at the SHADOW — never at the Sun. Place a small stone at the very tip of the shadow and note the time.
Every hour or two, come back and mark the new position of the shadow tip with another stone, writing the time beside it.
Continue through the day — morning, midday, and afternoon.
At the end of the day, look at the row of marks and the lengths of the shadows.
Safety: Never look directly at the sun — it can damage your eyes.

activities.title: Keeping a Moon Diary
activities.materials: A notebook or sheet of paper; A pencil; A clear view of the evening sky, with an adult; A calendar
steps: Each clear evening, go outside with an adult after sunset and find the Moon.
Draw the exact shape of the lit part of the Moon that you can see.
Write the date beside your drawing, and note roughly what time it was.
Repeat every clear night for at least two weeks — longer is even better.
If a night is cloudy, simply write 'cloudy' and try again the next night.

activities.title: Observe: Stars, Constellations and Finding Your Way
activities.materials: A ball (an orange, a round fruit, or any ball) to be Earth; A torch, or a phone light, to be the Sun; A small sticker or a dot of marker pen to mark your town; A darkened room
steps: Look for an example of stars, constellations and finding your way around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Earth's rotation (one spin) and Earth turning per hour.

rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the third. Earth is the third planet out from the Sun.

rounds.prompt: The Sun appears to rise in the ____ and set in the ____.
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: east, west. Because Earth spins west to east, the Sun appears to rise east and set west.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is NOT a planet in our Solar System?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the Sun. The Sun is a star, not a planet.

rounds.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin around once?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: 24 hours. One full spin (rotation) takes 24 hours, which is why a day is 24 hours.

games.title: Challenge Cards: Moon
games.description: Practise moon through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Why does the Moon shine?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: it reflects the Sun's light. The Moon makes no light of its own.

rounds.prompt: What is a star?
choices: a huge ball of hot glowing gas that makes its own light
rounds.answer: a huge ball of hot glowing gas that makes its own light
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: a huge ball of hot glowing gas that makes its own light. The Sun is our nearest star.

rounds.prompt: Why are stars useful to travellers at night?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: they help find direction. Certain stars point the way, like a natural compass.

rounds.prompt: What causes day and night?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Earth spinning on its axis. As Earth turns, your side faces the Sun (day) then turns away (night).

rounds.prompt: Which phase marks the start of a new month in the Islamic (Hijri) calendar?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: new crescent. The thin crescent after sunset marks the start of a Hijri month.

rounds.prompt: About how many days does the Moon take to complete all its phases?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: 29.5. The full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.

rounds.prompt: What is at the centre of our Solar System?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the Sun. The Sun sits at the centre and everything else orbits it.

rounds.prompt: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: about one year. One orbit of the Sun takes about 365 days.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit you will be able to:
I can explain that Earth is a planet that travels around the Sun, together with seven other planets in our Solar System.
I can describe how Earth spinning on its axis causes the cycle of day and night.
I can explain why the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, even though the Sun is not really moving around us.
I can describe how Earth's journey around the Sun takes one year (about 365 days).
I can explain why the Moon appears to change shape through its phases, and connect this to the lunar (Hijri) calendar.
I can name the eight planets in order and describe how the Solar System is arranged.
I can use the Sun and stars to work out direction, and understand how people have navigated with the sky.
